source: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving
finding: Founding study. People gave warmth ratings every so often. On multistep problems warmth rose step by step before the solution. On insight problems warmth stayed low and flat, then jumped. Warmth predicted success on multistep problems but not on insight problems.
numbers: Exact figures not read (paywall). A later critique reports only 39 of 73 subjects gave usable data (search snippet, unverified). Two scores used: differential warmth (last minus first rating) and angular warmth (change per second).
limits: Two different problem sets (insight vs multistep) differ in difficulty, steps and prior knowledge, so the contrast is confounded. Small usable sample. Not directly read this session.
agent_relevance: Source of the guardrail: a solver's own sense of closeness is blind on insight-type problems. Do not use self-reported warmth to decide when to switch.

source: Metcalfe (1986) Feeling of knowing in memory and problem solving; Premonitions of insight predict impending error
finding: Feeling-of-knowing predictions predicted later success on memory questions and on algebra problems, but not on insight problems. High premonitions on insight problems went with impending errors.
numbers: Per secondary sources (search results): correlation between predicted and actual solution was not different from zero for insight problems; substantial for memory questions. No exact r read.
limits: Secondary description only. Era of small samples and few items. Later work (b03-b08) shows the picture depends on how insight is defined.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that a confident, fluent feeling about an insight-type problem can mark an error, so the agent should not stop on its own confidence.

source: Hedne, Norman and Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: Conceptual re-test of Metcalfe and Wiebe with the same problems solved with or without self-reported insight (magic tricks). No warmth difference between insight and noninsight solutions: the 1987 pattern did not replicate.
numbers: N = 51 (8 dropped for no Aha), 971 trials, 29% insight. Differential warmth: insight M = 2.92 (SD 23.26, n = 50) vs noninsight M = 0.30 (SD 19.52, n = 162), t(210) = 0.79, p = .429, d = 0.12. Angular warmth d = 0.22, p = .266. Including last rating: d = 0.07 and 0.08.
quote: these findings contrast with the earlier findings of Metcalfe and Wiebe
limits: Magic tricks, one lab, many trials excluded (661 of 1632). Insight defined by self-report, a different operationalisation from 1987.
agent_relevance: Warmth is not a clean signature even in humans. Strengthens the rule to rely on code-detected impasse, not on felt progress.

source: Hedne et al. (2016), accuracy and confidence results
finding: Self-reported insight solutions were more often correct and more confident, yet confidence separated right from wrong only for noninsight solutions.
numbers: Accuracy: insight M = .57 (n = 281) vs noninsight .37 (n = 690), t(506.9) = 5.78, d = 0.51. Confidence 78.32 vs 68.95, d = 0.50. Confidence-accuracy Az: insight 0.56 (not different from 0.5, p = .142, d = 0.25); noninsight 0.64 (p < .001, d = 0.82). Insight vs noninsight Az difference n.s. (n = 33 pairs, p = .297).
limits: Az difference between types was not significant, so the claim 'blind on insight' rests on one test against chance. Confidence instruction did not mention confidence (a fix to earlier work).
agent_relevance: Even when insight solutions are right more often, confidence cannot tell right from wrong inside that group. Selection must be by running checks (G3, G5), not by stated confidence.

source: Hedne et al. (2016), recognition and perseveration
finding: People who had an insight were more likely to stick to an incorrect answer on a later recognition test.
numbers: Chose option most like written solution: insight M = 0.72 vs noninsight 0.61, d = 0.23, p = .001. Only when the written solution was wrong: 0.63 vs 0.51, d = 0.24, p = .017. When right: 0.79 vs 0.78 (no difference).
limits: Small effect. Self-report of strategy.
agent_relevance: A sudden 'got it' state makes a wrong answer sticky. Supports an independent re-check (S8) that does not see the first attempt.

source: Laukkonen and Tangen (2018) How to detect insight moments in problem solving experiments
finding: Direct test of whether the warmth measure and the Aha self-report find the same insights. They barely agree trial by trial. Warmth jumps do not tell whether someone reports an Aha.
numbers: N = 51 people; 180 correctly solved problems with 2+ warmth ratings (182 in the correlation). Per-person count of self-reported vs warmth insights r = .61; per-problem r = .08 (p = .235). If warmth jumped, 75.6% reported Aha; if warmth was gradual, 50.8% still reported Aha.
limits: Only correct solutions analysed. Self-report was treated as the standard, which is a theoretical choice. Warmth can look gradual while the real shift is sudden (they argue illusory progress).
agent_relevance: Two human measures of 'insight' disagree, so no single felt signal should gate behaviour. Use observable events (no pass, repeated error, no change).

source: Danek and Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha! experience along its multiple dimensions for correct and incorrect solutions
finding: False insights exist: strong Aha ratings often go with wrong solutions. Aha was higher for correct solutions but with large overlap.
numbers: N = 70, 37 magic tricks, 1778 solutions (36.8% correct). Aha 66.50 (SD 18.42) correct vs 52.34 (SD 18.78) incorrect, t(69) = 10.21. 37% (417 of 1124) of incorrect solutions had Aha above the correct-solution mean. Solution time 35.81 s correct vs 42.46 s incorrect. Aha predicted by Pleasure, Suddenness, Certainty.
limits: Magic tricks, one lab. Correctness scored by the experimenters.
agent_relevance: Feeling of insight is a leaky but real signal; it should be a hint at most. A fast, confident wrong answer is the dangerous case, so check fast answers too.

source: Kizilirmak, Serger, Kehl, Ollinger, Folta-Schoofs and Richardson-Klavehn (2018) Feelings-of-warmth increase more abruptly for verbal riddles solved with in contrast to without Aha! experience
finding: Partial support for Metcalfe and Wiebe: with remote-associate riddles, warmth rose more steeply just before the solution when the solver reported Aha than when not.
numbers: N about 36 (df 35). Last minus third-to-last warmth: 2.59 (SD 0.97) with Aha vs 1.43 (SD 1.07) without, t(26) = 4.27, d = 0.82. Interaction round x Aha F(2,52) = 15.63, partial eta-squared = .375. P(Aha | generated) = .76 vs .57 for presented solutions. Aha rate did not depend on difficulty.
limits: Warmth rose in both groups; the difference is the size of the last jump, not flat vs rising. Only problems solved after 3+ rounds. Also, Aha was reported for about half of unsolved (presented) problems.
agent_relevance: The late jump is real but weak as a predictor: warmth still increases before every solution, so a 'warmth is flat' alarm is not a reliable impasse detector.

source: Salvi, Bricolo, Kounios, Bowden and Beeman (2016) Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions
finding: Across four experiments, self-judged insight solutions were more often correct than analytic ones. Analytic solutions had more commission errors.
numbers: Per press releases (not verified): 94% vs 78% correct on linguistic puzzles; 78% vs 42% on visual puzzles.
limits: Full text not read. Press-release numbers only.
agent_relevance: Insight feeling carries real information about correctness, so the guardrail is not 'ignore it'; it is 'do not use it to decide when to stop or switch'.

source: Laukkonen, Kaveladze, Tangen and Schooler (2020) The dark side of Eureka: artificially induced Aha moments make facts feel true
finding: Preregistered. An Aha from solving an anagram raised truth ratings of unrelated statements, even false ones. The insight feeling spills over onto neighbouring ideas.
numbers: n = 300 recruited, 268 analysed. Solved vs unsolved anagram: d = .609. Aha vs no Aha: d = .629. Solved with Aha 7.2 vs without 6.31 on truth ratings, d = .321. Insight rate 39%; insight anagrams more correct (.71 vs .50, d = .48).
limits: Anagrams, online sample, statements unrelated to the anagram. Truth ratings, not real decisions.
agent_relevance: A feeling attached to one thought raises belief in the next. Supports fresh-context judging with no authorship cue (G5) and no self-confidence carryover.

source: Grimmer, Laukkonen, Freydenzon, von Hippel and Tangen (2022) Thinking style and psychosis proneness do not predict false insights
finding: The FIAT paradigm (visually or semantically primed wrong anagram answers) induces false insights in most people. Thinking style and psychosis proneness measures did not predict who has them.
numbers: From the earlier FIAT study cited there: 9.3% of people had no false insight, 1.3% had one on every primed lure, 44.6% had false insights on at least half the trials. Max six false insights per person.
limits: Null result for the individual-difference predictors. Anagram task only. FIAT rates are quoted from the earlier paper, not measured here.
agent_relevance: False insight is common and not tied to a trait, so it cannot be screened out by choosing a 'careful' persona. Verify with code.

source: Grimmer et al. (2023) The illusion of insight: detailed warnings reduce but do not prevent false Aha moments
finding: Simple warnings did not cut false insights. A detailed explanation of the trick gave only a small reduction.
numbers: Per search summary only; no numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Abstract-level information from a search snippet.
agent_relevance: Telling a solver 'be careful, you may be fooled' barely helps. Matches the schema section 4b point that debiasing instructions fail.

source: Ammalainen and Moroshkina (2020) When an error leads to confidence: false insight and feeling of knowing in anagram solving
finding: Anagrams hiding a shorter word: a picture of the shorter word caused many intrusion errors, and feeling of knowing was higher after a fast wrong answer.
numbers: N = 43 (28 in FOK analysis). Intrusion errors 25 after interfering prime vs 1 (irrelevant) and 2 (neutral), F(2,84) = 15.7. FOK1 3.05 (SD 1.49) after a wrong first answer vs 2.67 (SD 1.27) without, chi-sq(2) = 15.4. FOK did not differ by prime type.
limits: Small N. Aha not measured. Read via a web summarizer of the page, not the paper PDF. Year taken from the summary, unverified.
agent_relevance: A wrong, quickly produced answer raises the felt chance of success. The first plausible answer should not be trusted just because it feels close.

source: Becker, Wang and Cabeza (2024) Surprise! Clarifying the link between insight and prediction error
finding: Preregistered online test of a metacognitive prediction-error account. Aha was linked to being surprised that a problem turned out solvable, not to timing. Suddenness related negatively.
numbers: n = 39 after exclusions (45 recruited), compound remote associates, mean accuracy 51.0% (SD 24.4%), solution time 10.5 s. Surprise tracked the solvability prediction error; pleasure, certainty and suddenness did not.
limits: Small sample, brief report, verbal problems only. Solvability predictions were made before solving.
agent_relevance: People do make advance guesses about solvability and the Aha tracks how wrong they were. A solver's prior on difficulty is not a clean signal either; budget by difficulty class from data (G12).

source: Rebus-puzzle study (2024) The Aha! experience is associated with a drop in the perceived difficulty of the problem
finding: Initial difficulty ratings (within 5 s) predicted whether people would fail and how long they took. Stronger Aha went with a larger drop from initial to retrospective difficulty, and faster solutions for hard-seeming items.
numbers: N = 160, rebus puzzles, 7-point scales. 58% correct, 23% incorrect. Initial difficulty: correct 3.45, incorrect 4.63, unsolved 5.54 (beta 0.95 and 1.53, p < .001). Correct solutions 7.10 s vs incorrect 17.3 s.
limits: Rebus puzzle sets; the quick initial rating is a prediction made after seeing the puzzle, not during solving.
agent_relevance: Early difficulty judgments do carry signal, so a cheap pre-solve gate (S0) is plausible, but it is a different thing from mid-solve closeness (warmth).

source: McGuinness, Schooler, Gable and Gross (2026) The Aha! Glow: insight experiences bias judgements of idea quality in divergent contexts
finding: Boundary condition on the insight-accuracy link. On a convergent task insight predicts accuracy. On an open-ended task insight inflates self-rated creativity far more than objective creativity.
numbers: Study 2: N = 100 (Prolific). CRAT accuracy: within-person b = 0.65, OR = 1.92 (95% CI 1.82-2.03); between-person OR = 1.13 (p = .046). AUT: insight vs self-rated creativity within-person partial R2 = 0.17; vs objective creativity b = 0.08 (between-person n.s., b = 0.02, p = .33). Bias score (self minus objective) b = 0.19, partial R2 = 0.064. Study 1: diary data, 45 physicists and 53 writers; writers downgraded Aha ideas at 6 months.
limits: Online sample, AUT scored by trained raters. Study 1 is a re-analysis of older data.
agent_relevance: In open (divergent) mode, the generating model's sense of a good idea is biased upward. Supports G8: judge novelty by running or outside raters, never by the generator.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal fundamental limits of machine insight and self-evaluation (NazoNazo benchmark)
finding: 38 frontier LLMs on insight-like riddles in a retrieval-free zero-shot setting. Models are far below people on accuracy and show 'verification failure': a correct candidate appears in the thinking log but is not endorsed as the answer.
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference on 120 items, n = 126, mean 52.9%. Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6% on that subset. GPT-5 within the 95% CI of the human mean. Verification failures were 5.23% to 39.34% of incorrect answers across four models with usable logs (Gemini 2.5 Flash 5.23%, Grok 4 39.34%).
limits: Observational; verification failure counted only when the gold answer appears verbatim in the log; only four models had usable thought logs; Japanese-language items. GPT-5 comparison does not prove equivalence.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S4 harvest: code must extract every candidate raised in an attempt and test them all, because the model's own endorsement drops correct ones.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025), model-by-model table
finding: Model thought logs also showed wrong answers adopted with apparent confidence after a reinterpretation, besides the continued-search pattern. Accuracy varied by language for some models.
numbers: Example: Grok-4 correct share of answered 29.5% (33/112) in Japanese vs 48.8% (40/82) in English, Fisher p = .0071. Claude Opus 4: 36.7% (16/44) vs 28.7% (45/157), p = .356.
limits: Per-model counts are small. Missing thought logs excluded from denominators.
agent_relevance: Large variation by language and model means any internal stop signal must be validated per setting before it is used.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Understanding Aha moments: from external observations to internal mechanisms
finding: Studies 'aha moments' in reasoning models via language, uncertainty and latent states. Claims aha moments show as more human-like self-reflection wording and adjusted uncertainty by difficulty, and that models avoid 'reasoning collapse' (no final answer).
numbers: Only the abstract and section headings were read; no effect sizes extracted. Tasks included Countdown and Knights-and-Knaves puzzles with difficulty levels.
limits: Aha is defined by reflective wording, not by a human-style sudden shift; no test that these words predict correctness. Analysis only skimmed.
agent_relevance: The 'aha' wording in a model's trace is not the human insight signal and should not trigger anything in our scaffold.

source: Thinking Out Loud: Do reasoning models know when they are right? (2025)
finding: Verbalized confidence of reasoning models improves with distillation and RL in reasoning-heavy settings, but small reasoning models may be worse at recognizing the limits of their knowledge.
numbers: Compared instruct, SFT and RL models; larger RL models better aligned. SimpleQA/FreshQA 'not attempted' counts: 14B instruct 1136 vs 102 (SFT) and 103 (RL); 32B 2492 vs 76 vs 63.
limits: Factual and math benchmarks, not insight tasks. Only the abstract and results text were read.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence is better after RL, but still a hint (G4, G10). Not a replacement for external checks.

source: Trace length is a simple uncertainty signal in reasoning models (2025)
finding: Reasoning-trace length predicts correctness about as well as verbalized confidence, and the two are complementary; the link survives controls for difficulty and a length bias from RL training.
numbers: Measured by AUROC across models and datasets; specific values not extracted (abstract and method read). Mechanism linked to high-entropy forking tokens.
limits: Not insight problems. Numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: A code-measurable proxy (length, or a budget fraction spent) beats asking the model how close it feels, which fits the S6 trigger of budget used.

source: Reported confidence in LLMs tracks commitment more than correctness (2026)
finding: A two-stage test: model answers and states confidence, then decides to commit or abstain. Verbal confidence predicted the commit decision much better than correctness. Token log-probabilities tracked correctness.
numbers: Four non-reasoning models, replicated on four reasoning models and four benchmarks. After removing the part of verbal confidence shared with calibrated log-probabilities, residual verbal confidence had mean AUROC = 0.473 for correctness (W = 11, p = .844 vs 0.5) while residual log-probability kept 0.686.
limits: Preprint. Mechanistic part on Gemma models only. Not an insight task.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to the human finding: self-reported closeness or confidence reflects a drive to commit, not evidence. Strong support for the guardrail.

source: Reasoning about uncertainty: do reasoning models know when they don't know? (2025)
finding: Reasoning models are poorly calibrated, mostly overconfident, especially on hard question sets. Calibration was good on easy sets such as ARC-Challenge and MMLU subsets.
numbers: Reported as ECE and MCE per benchmark and prompt strategy (basic, chain-of-thought, multi-step, top-K with K = 5); exact values not extracted.
limits: Only a part of the paper was read; knowledge benchmarks, not insight problems.
agent_relevance: Overconfidence grows where the problem is hard, which is where an agent would need a stop or switch signal. Another reason to move that decision to code.

source: Webb, Laukkonen, Cropper and Little (2021) commentary on the insight-accuracy link (Journal of Creative Behavior)
finding: Argues the Aha-accuracy link is real but overstated and that there are reasons for caution about a general accuracy advantage of insight solutions.
numbers: None read.
limits: Known only from a search summary; not opened.
agent_relevance: Competing view to treat as a caution: accuracy advantage may come from task selection and error types, not from insight itself.

source: Laukkonen, Webb, Salvi, Tangen, Slagter and Schooler (2023) Insight and the selection of ideas (Eureka heuristic)
finding: Proposes that the feeling of insight is a fast metacognitive heuristic for choosing which idea reaches awareness and gets acted on. It works when implicit knowledge is sound and fails when it is corrupted.
numbers: None read.
limits: Review; known from search summary and from citations in opened papers (b10, b16).
agent_relevance: A theory that fits b04, b07, b10 and b16: the feeling selects ideas, so an agent that copies it needs an outside check on the selected idea.

source: Rival-theory contrast built from Hedne 2016, Laukkonen and Tangen 2018, Kizilirmak 2018
finding: Two views of closeness feelings: continuous (feeling grows slowly then crosses awareness) vs discontinuous (no growth before a sudden jump). Data: Kizilirmak finds a bigger last-step jump with Aha (d = 0.82) but warmth rises in both; Hedne finds no difference (d = 0.12); Laukkonen and Tangen find warmth shape unrelated to Aha reports (r = .08).
numbers: As in b03, b06, b08. No study used a large preregistered sample.
limits: Different tasks (magic, riddles, remote associates), different definitions of insight, small N. No discriminating experiment with a shared protocol has been run.
agent_relevance: The honest summary: warmth works as a weak marker of a late jump, not as a predictor of success. This does not change the guardrail.

source: Hedne et al. (2016), methodological moderators discussion
finding: Hedne et al. list why results differ: pre-defined insight problem sets confound insight with difficulty and prior knowledge, and earlier instructions told participants Aha means confidence. Both can create the insight-confidence link by demand.
numbers: Their fix: no confidence wording in the Aha instruction; confidence still higher for insight (78.32 vs 68.95, d = 0.50).
limits: One study. No data on time pressure, training, expertise or culture in the sources opened this session.
agent_relevance: No evidence found that instruction or training makes people better at judging closeness on insight problems; nothing to add to the schema. Gap for a later pass.

source: Gap record for Angle B (interventions, expertise, culture)
finding: In the sources opened, no intervention was found that improved the accuracy of closeness or Aha-based monitoring. The best-evidenced remedy is external: make the shift observable (Laukkonen and Tangen propose a dynamometer grip measure) or check the answer.
numbers: None. Detailed warnings reduced false insights only slightly (b12, unopened).
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search; Metcalfe 1986/1987 text, Weisberg 1992 and the meta-reviews were not reachable.
agent_relevance: Do not add a self-monitoring prompt as an operator. Keep monitoring in code (outputs, repeat errors, budget).
